title: The Treasurer's Flight: Baghdad to Bombay, and the House That Followed the Trade Winds
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Baghdad, birth in the treasurer's house
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1792; no source gives the day of the month, which is defaulted to the first
stops.campa: A son is born to Sheikh Sassoon ben Saleh, chief treasurer to the pashas of Baghdad and head of the city's Jews, and to his wife Amam Gabbai. The house he enters is not a merchant's house but an office. The sarraf bashi keeps the governor's money, farms his revenues, and answers with his own neck for the arithmetic. The boy is raised to the ledger and to the Book together, in Hebrew and Arabic and Turkish, inside a community that has prayed on this river since the exile. He takes his father's given name for a surname, in the manner of the place.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Ottoman Baghdad and the office of sarraf bashi under the Mamluk governors

stops.name: Baghdad, the seat at the pasha's counting table
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1817-1829; the sources give no month for his assumption of the office
stops.campa: At twenty-five he takes his father's work as his own, sarraf bashi to the Ottoman governors of Baghdad, banker to a pashalik that pays its soldiers late and its creditors later. The office is honor and hostage at once. No Jew in the city stands higher, and none stands nearer the executioner. He learns in it the two skills the rest of his life will run on: how to move money between currencies and jurisdictions, and how to read the temper of a ruler before the ruler has finished speaking.
suggested_refs: The revenue-farming system of the Baghdad pashalik under the last Mamluk walis

stops.name: Baghdad, the first marriage and the second son
stops.date_confidence: marriage attested to 1818; Elias's birth attested to 27 March 1820, the date carried here
stops.campa: He marries Hannah Joseph in 1818, and on the twenty-seventh of March 1820 she bears him Elias, second of the four children she will give him. That boy will be sent east at twenty-four to open China for his father's house, and will end by founding a rival to it. For now he is an infant in a treasurer's household in the Jewish quarter, among people who keep the Sabbath, the tithe, and the accounts of a Mamluk governor, and who have no reason yet to picture themselves living in any other city.
suggested_refs: Baghdadi Jewish marriage and inheritance practice in the early nineteenth century

stops.name: Baghdad, the last of the slave governors
stops.date_confidence: Dawud Pasha ruled to 1831; the persecution is dated by the sources only to the later years of his rule, and the stop is placed at mid-decade
stops.campa: Dawud Pasha, last of the Mamluk governors of Baghdad, rules the city and squeezes it. He takes what he wants from the Jewish notables and then takes it again; extortion runs into imprisonment, imprisonment into flight. The Sassoons are the richest and most exposed family in the community, holding the governor's money and therefore holding his suspicion. The father is past eighty, the son in his thirties. Neither can lay the office down without confessing to a fortune, and neither can hold it and be safe.
stops.quote: Daoud Pasha was not only the last, but also the most tyrannical of the Slave Governors. His maltreatment of the Jews in his Pashalik was particularly brutal.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 33
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 33
suggested_refs: Dawud Pasha of Baghdad and the end of Mamluk rule in Iraq, 1831

stops.name: Baghdad, a wife buried and a wife married
stops.date_confidence: Hannah's death attested to 1826, the second marriage to 1828; the stop carries the later date
stops.campa: Hannah Joseph dies in 1826 and leaves him four children. In 1828 he marries Farha Hyeem, who will bear him ten more, and whose sons will carry the name to Shanghai, to Hong Kong, and to a house in Kent. He remarries in the same season that the governor's persecution closes on the household, while the family is turning what it holds into a form that can travel. Fourteen children in all, eight of them sons. Every branch office the house ever opens will be run by one of them.
suggested_refs: The second wife's name is given variously as Farha Hyeem and Farha Hai Gubbay

stops.name: Baghdad, the order to hang the treasurer
stops.date_confidence: 1829 per Roth; Roth himself footnotes other and less dramatic accounts of why Sassoon left Baghdad, and no contemporary document was reachable
stops.campa: Word of what the Sassoons have done, or have been accused of doing, reaches the governor. He orders the hanging of the man who keeps his accounts, and turns on the community behind him with a persecution more methodical than any before it. Roth, telling the story eighty years later, appends a footnote conceding that other and less dramatic reasons for the departure were also told. In either telling the outcome is the same: the treasurer of Baghdad cannot stay in Baghdad and live.
stops.quote: But in the meantime, in 1829, the news of what had happened became known in the city. The Vali swore revenge, began a thorough-going persecution of the Jews on a more systematic plan than before, and, of course, gave orders for this arch-enemy to be hanged.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 33
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 33
suggested_refs: Roth's footnote at p. 33 admitting competing accounts of the flight

stops.name: Baghdad, the escape by night
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Roth gives the night flight with his own hedge, probably assisted by disguise and bribery, and the month is unrecorded
stops.campa: By night, with his father who is past eighty beside him, David Sassoon goes out of the city his family has banked for two generations. Roth's account gives him a disguise and money at the gate. Nothing of the escape survives in a document written at the time. He carries no office and no protection out of the gate, and takes downriver whatever gold can be moved without being noticed. He is thirty-six. Everything he becomes afterward is built by a man who has already lost one country.
stops.quote: Accompanied by his octogenarian father, and probably assisted by disguise and judicious bribery, David Sassoon escaped from Baghdad by night.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 34
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 34
suggested_refs: The gates and river quays of Ottoman Baghdad, route of the 1829 flight

stops.name: Basra, the road to the sea
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the flight route is described only in general terms, no reachable source names Basra directly, and the month is invented for ordering only
stops.campa: The road out of Ottoman Iraq runs down the Tigris to Basra and the head of the Gulf, the port through which Baghdad's money has always reached open water. Tradition puts the family through it. No source consulted names a house, a date, or a boat. What is certain is only the direction. From here the Sassoons stop being the subjects of a pasha and become a cargo, moving on the same water road that Indian pepper and Gulf pearls have used for a thousand years.
sources: Reconstructed from the general flight route in Wikipedia, 'Sassoon family'
suggested_refs: The Shatt al-Arab and the Basra-to-Bushehr coasting trade

stops.name: Bushehr, trading again outside the pasha's reach
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1828 or 1829 depending on the article, with the residence running to 1832; the month is unrecorded and is set for ordering only
stops.campa: At Bushehr on the Persian shore, outside the pasha's reach and inside the East India Company's, he sets up again as a merchant. The Gulf port is a clearing house for Indian cottons, Arabian horses, dates, and pearls, and the Baghdadi Jewish network that works it already knows his name. For three or four years he trades here and watches where the money comes from. Everything that arrives worth having arrives out of Bombay, under a flag that does not hang its bankers.
suggested_refs: Bushehr as the East India Company's Gulf residency and entrepot

stops.name: Bushehr, the death of Sassoon ben Saleh
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the place of death is not, and is given only as probably Bushehr or the Basra region, with no grave named
stops.campa: Sassoon ben Saleh dies in exile, chief treasurer of Baghdad no longer, four decades of office ended in a rented room on the Persian coast. The sources do not agree on where he lies, and none names the grave. With the old man's death the last obligation holding the household to the Gulf is gone. Within two years his son will be in India, and the family's center of gravity will never come back to the two rivers. The office that made them is not inherited by anyone again.
suggested_refs: Jewish burial grounds of Bushehr and Basra, unlocated for this family

stops.name: Bombay, landing as a refugee at forty
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He lands at Bombay with his family, a refugee at forty, in a city the British have made out of seven islands and a customs house. He has Arabic, Hebrew, Turkish, and Persian, and no English worth the name. What he has instead is a correspondent in every Gulf and Mesopotamian port that matters, and a standing among them older than any counting house on this shore. Bombay is not yet the first port of India. He lands in the decade it begins to become one, while the water frontage is still cheap.
suggested_refs: The Fort of Bombay and its merchant communities in the 1830s

stops.name: 9 Tamarind Street, the house in the Fort
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the address is given in the sources but the building is not extant and the plot is locatable only to the Fort district
stops.campa: The household takes a house at 9 Tamarind Street in the Fort, a Baghdadi family among Parsis, Gujaratis, and Englishmen, keeping its own rite in its own language. He wears the turban and robes of a Baghdad notable to the end of his life, keeps the Sabbath strictly, and hires a teacher to give him working Hindustani so that he can deal with the men on the wharf himself. His sons will wear English clothes and English manners. He permits it, and does not imitate it.
suggested_refs: Tamarind Lane, Fort, Bombay, the family's first address in India

stops.name: Bombay, David Sassoon and Company
stops.date_confidence: the firm was founded 1832 and he was among the wealthiest men in India by the 1830s; the stop is placed mid-decade to carry the method rather than a dated event
stops.campa: The firm opens as a middleman: Manchester textiles out into the Gulf, Persian and Mesopotamian wool, silk, spices, and pearls back. He takes his profits out of goods and puts them into the harbor itself, wharves and godowns and water frontage, so that the trade of other men pays him rent. He staffs the counting house with Baghdadi Jews brought out from Iraq and Persia, schools their children at his own cost, and gives away the tenth as the law requires. By the 1830s he is among the richest men in India.
stops.quote: the employment of his sons as his agents and to his strict observance of the law of tithe
stops.quote_source: Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906), 'Sassoon', on the reasons David Sassoon himself gave for his success
suggested_refs: The godowns and wharves of the Bombay harbor front acquired in the 1830s

stops.name: Bombay, the oath signed in Hebrew
stops.date_confidence: 1853 attested; the Poona setting given in some retellings is unsupported, his base that year being Bombay, and no month is recorded
stops.campa: He becomes a British subject and signs the Oath of Allegiance to Queen Victoria in Hebrew letters, having no English to sign it in. The gesture is exact. He takes the protection of the empire whose ships and courts have made the fortune possible, and signs for it in the alphabet of the community that made him. The document binds a fugitive from Ottoman Baghdad to the crown that will make his sons baronets, and it is the only signature of his that most of his own clerks could not read.
suggested_refs: The 1853 Oath of Allegiance signed in Hebrew script

stops.name: Sans Souci, Byculla, the house that becomes a hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested to the middle decades of the century; the year of the move from the Fort is not given in any reachable source
stops.campa: He leaves the Fort for Byculla and a former palace called Sans Souci, where the garden runs down toward the tank and the household keeps Baghdad hours in an English suburb. Visitors describe a court rather than a drawing room: petitioners out of the community, rabbis from Ottoman Palestine collecting for the poor of Jerusalem, agents in from Bushehr and Basra, the old man in his turban hearing all of them. The house will outlive him as a hospital. He is the head of a congregation before he is a rich man.
suggested_refs: Sans Souci, Byculla, afterwards the Masina Hospital

stops.name: Hong Kong, a branch on the new island
stops.date_confidence: 1843 per the firm's own branch list; several accounts give 1844 and tie the opening to Elias's voyage, which the earlier date rules out, and a third source gives 1858
stops.campa: The Treaty of Nanking opens the Chinese coast and cedes an island, and the firm puts a branch on it. Hong Kong is a garrison and a harbor with hardly any town yet, and the Sassoon office exists there to do one thing: move Malwa opium out of Bombay into a market the Royal Navy has just forced open, and move silver back. The branch is standing before any of his sons reaches China. He is running the eastern trade from a desk in Bombay, by letter, in Baghdadi Arabic written in Hebrew characters that no rival house can read.
suggested_refs: The branch list of David Sassoon & Co. and its conflicting dates for Hong Kong

stops.name: Canton, the second son at the factories
stops.date_confidence: 1844 attested for Elias's arrival; no month is given
stops.campa: Twelve years into Bombay, the father sends the second son east to see the trade for himself. Elias David Sassoon, twenty-four years old, lands at Canton among the factories on the riverfront where the whole China trade has been penned for a century, and finds the place already half emptied of its importance by the new treaty ports to the north. He stays long enough to learn the market and the men in it. The house built on the Gulf network is about to be rebuilt on a longer line, with a son of the founder standing at each end of it.
stops.quote: As a result, in 1844, after he had been settled in Bombay for a little more than ten years, he had the idea of dispatching one of his sons to the Far East to supervise the operations of the firm. It was the second and (apparently) most enterprising of the house, Elias, whom he chose for the purpose.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 48
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 48
suggested_refs: The Thirteen Factories quarter of Canton after the Treaty of Nanking

stops.name: Shanghai, the office on the mudflats
stops.date_confidence: 1845 attested for the move north; no month is given
stops.campa: Elias moves the China business north to Shanghai, where the Yangtze meets the sea and the British concession is being staked out on mudflats along the Bund. He judges that everything Canton has will pass to this place, and it does. The office opens on the waterfront, and the family's ships will carry, at the height of the trade, something near a fifth of all the opium landed in China, with tea, silk, and silver going the other way. His elder brother Albert works the Bombay end. The two ends are one house.
suggested_refs: The British concession at Shanghai and the first Bund godowns

stops.name: Bombay, the trade that turns in three motions
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1840s and 1850s as a pattern rather than as a dated event; the stop is placed at mid-century
stops.campa: The machine turns in three motions. Indian opium and raw cotton go east to China; silver, tea, and silk come back to Bombay; English manufactures come out from Lancashire and are sold across India on the same account. Each leg pays for the next, and the family owns ships, wharves, and warehouses at every corner, so that no freight or storage charge leaks away to a stranger. Eight sons are stationed along the line. No part of the chain is handled by a man who is not a Sassoon.
stops.quote: the most lucrative part of the trade from British India to China and beyond (and, later on, much of the direct trade from England to the Far East) came into the hands of the firm of David Sassoon, Sons, & Company
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 49
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 49
suggested_refs: The Bombay-China-London triangular trade in opium, cotton, and manufactures

stops.name: London, the other end of the line
stops.date_confidence: c. 1858 per Roth's narrative order; the sources give no precise date for the London opening
stops.campa: The house opens in London, and with London come Liverpool and Manchester, the cotton ports at the far end of the route. The move changes what the firm is. It is no longer an Indian merchant selling into England, but an English house trading on its own account from both ends. A son goes over to run it. From here begins the passage from Bombay notable to English gentry that will finish in a baronetcy, a seat in the Commons, and a poet writing in Kent about the Western Front.
stops.quote: London now became a main centre of the firm's operations, and as a natural consequence branches were established also in Liverpool and Manchester.
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 50
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 50
suggested_refs: The London, Liverpool, and Manchester branches of David Sassoon, Sons & Co.

stops.name: Bombay, the cotton famine
stops.date_confidence: the American Civil War cotton boom ran 1861-1865; the stop is dated to its opening year
stops.campa: The American war closes the southern ports and Lancashire starves for cotton. Bombay, which has grown the crop for a century as a second-rate substitute, becomes for four years the only supply on earth, and the price of Indian raw cotton goes up several times over. The Sassoon house sits exactly where the money passes, holding the presses, the godowns, the ships, and the London end together. Fortunes are made in Bombay in these years that outlast the men who make them. His is one, and it is already the largest.
suggested_refs: The Bombay cotton boom of 1861-1865 and the share mania that followed it

stops.name: Bombay, the sons at their books
stops.date_confidence: the visitor's remark is dated 1854 by Roth; no month is given
stops.campa: A visitor out of Ottoman Palestine, collecting for the poor of the Holy Land, is taken through the household and sees the sons at their studies. They are being schooled in the traditional Baghdadi way, Hebrew and the commentaries first, with whatever English and accountancy the firm requires laid on top and never in place of it. The visitor writes down what he sees with delight. Within thirty years these same boys will sit in Brighton drawing rooms and in the House of Commons, and one of them will be made a baronet.
stops.quote: All of them are pious and learned
stops.quote_source: an ecstatic visitor from Palestine, 1854, quoted in Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 55
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 55
suggested_refs: Roth at p. 55 on the traditional Jewish education of David Sassoon's eight sons

stops.name: Byculla, the museum of three merchants
stops.date_confidence: established 1855, opened to the public as the Victoria and Albert Museum on 2 May 1872, renamed 1 November 1975; the stop is dated to the founding
stops.campa: A museum is founded in the Byculla gardens on the subscriptions of the city's merchant princes, David Sassoon among them, beside Sir Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy the Parsi and Jagannath Shunkerseth the Hindu. Three communities that share no scripture put their money on the same building. It opens as the Victoria and Albert Museum, Bombay, and a century later takes the name of Dr Bhau Daji Lad. He endows what the whole city uses, and endows separately what only his own people use.
suggested_refs: The Victoria and Albert Museum, Byculla, now the Dr Bhau Daji Lad Museum

stops.name: Bombay, the Benevolent Institution
stops.date_confidence: founded in the 1850s; no reachable source gives a precise year, and the stop is dated to mid-decade
stops.campa: He founds the David Sassoon Benevolent Institution to school the poor Jews coming into Bombay behind him out of Baghdad, Basra, Bushehr, and Aleppo, drawn by the news that a Baghdadi in India can prosper without a governor's leave. The school teaches Hebrew, English, and a trade. The community assembling around it speaks Arabic, prays in the Baghdadi rite, and lives under British law in a Hindu and Muslim city. He governs it as his father governed the Jews of Baghdad, which is to say by paying for it.
suggested_refs: The David Sassoon Benevolent Institution and the Baghdadi migration to Bombay

stops.name: Bombay, as an English official sees him
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source, stated only as before 1864; the stop is placed near the end of his life
stops.campa: Richard Temple, an officer of the Bombay government, is presented to the old merchant and writes down what he sees: a figure in turban and flowing robes, grave, upright, past sixty and unmistakable in a room of frock coats. A second description of him survives on the same page of the same book with no name attached to it. He has been a British subject for seven years and has taken up not one English habit of dress or diet. His sons, in the next room, are dressed like the men describing him.
stops.quote: He was then advanced in years, and his grave countenance, commanding figure, rich turban and flowing robes made up a picture worth beholding.
stops.quote_source: Sir Richard Temple, quoted in Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 53
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 53
suggested_refs: Temple's memoir was not located; the description survives only through Roth's quotation

stops.name: Magen David Synagogue, Byculla
stops.date_confidence: contested: Roth and one Wikipedia line give 1861, the article on the synagogue itself gives a construction year of 1864; the conflict is left open
stops.campa: He builds the community its synagogue in Byculla, a large hall in a walled compound with a clock tower over the gate, paid for out of his own purse. The Baghdadi rite is kept in it exactly as it was kept on the Tigris, the same melodies and the same Arabic pronunciation, and the congregation that fills it is one he has largely brought over and employed. His grandson Jacob will extend the building fifty years on. It is the first thing he founds that is meant to outlast the firm, and it does.
stops.quote: In 1861, David Sassoon built it a beautiful synagogue in the then fashionable Byculla quarter, set in a spacious compound and equipped with a clock-tower
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 59
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 59
suggested_refs: Magen David Synagogue, 340 Sir J.J. Road, Byculla, extended c. 1910 by Jacob Sassoon

stops.name: Byculla, the hospice, the bath, and the Talmud Torah
stops.date_confidence: attested to the years around the synagogue's building, c. 1861-1864; no separate founding dates are given
stops.campa: Around the synagogue he sets the rest of what a Jewish community requires: a hospice for travelers coming down the Gulf road, a ritual bath, a Talmud Torah for the boys. To these are added over the same years dispensaries, a library, a burial ground, and pensions for the widows of men who worked in the house. Out of a trading firm's cash box he is running the whole civil apparatus of a nation with no territory. No state anywhere is answerable for these people. He is.
stops.quote: he erected a hospice for travellers, a ritual bath, and a Talmud Torah, or institution for the education of Jewish youth
stops.quote_source: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 59
sources: Cecil Roth, The Sassoon Dynasty (1941), p. 59
suggested_refs: The charitable trusts attached to the Byculla synagogue compound

stops.name: Poona, the hot-weather house
stops.date_confidence: attested that his later years were based partly at Poona; no year of settlement is given
stops.campa: In his last years he keeps to Poona above the ghats, where the Bombay merchant class goes to escape the coast in the hot months and where the army has its cantonment. He is past seventy. The firm runs itself out of Bombay, Shanghai, Hong Kong, and London in his sons' hands, and the letters come up to him. What he does with the time left is build, in a town he did not make his money in, the same set of institutions he built below: a synagogue, a school, a library, a hospital, a house for the destitute.
suggested_refs: The Camp quarter of Poona and its Bombay merchant summer residents

stops.name: Poona, the home for the old and destitute
stops.date_confidence: 1863 attested; no month is given
stops.campa: He founds a home in Poona for the aged and the destitute, one year before his own death at seventy-two. It is not a Jewish charity only. The synagogue and the Talmud Torah are for his own community; the hospital, the library, the mechanics' institute, and the poorhouse are for whoever in the city needs them, out of the same account and under the same name. The Baghdad office taught him what a community without a protector is worth. He spends forty years being one.
suggested_refs: The David Sassoon Elderly and Destitute Persons Home, Poona

stops.name: Poona, ground broken for the red temple
stops.date_confidence: construction attested to 1863-1867; the month is unrecorded
stops.campa: Ground is broken in the Camp for a synagogue in red brick, Gothic revival, with a spire and a clock, designed by an officer of the Royal Engineers named Henry Saint Clair Wilkins. Poona will call it the Laal Deval, the red temple, and will go on calling it that long after the congregation has gone. He does not live to see it consecrated. It is the largest synagogue anyone raises in Asia outside the land of Israel, built by a man who left Baghdad with what he could carry, for a congregation that never much exceeds a hundred families.
suggested_refs: Ohel David Synagogue, Moledina Grant Road, Camp, Poona; architect Henry Saint Clair Wilkins

stops.name: Poona, the death of David Sassoon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 November 1864
stops.campa: He dies at Poona on the seventh of November, aged seventy-two, thirty-five years after going out of Baghdad by night with only what could be carried unnoticed. He leaves eight sons stationed from the Bund to the City of London, a firm moving a fifth of the opium entering China, wharves and mills in Bombay, and a community of several thousand people who are in India because he made a place for them. He is buried in the compound of his own unfinished synagogue, under a Gothic canopy, facing Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: The mausoleum of David Sassoon in the Ohel David compound, by Henry Saint Clair Wilkins

stops.name: Poona, the Laal Deval consecrated over his grave
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 September 1867
stops.campa: Three years after his death the synagogue is finished by his sons and consecrated, with the mausoleum standing inside the compound wall so that the congregation walks past the founder to reach the ark. The building holds. The congregation does not: a hundred families at its height, a remnant by the end of the next century, the doors locked for security and opened by arrangement, the services kept by laymen and visiting cantors. The grave stays where it was put, in a city whose largest hospital still carries his name.
suggested_refs: Ohel David, described as the largest synagogue in Asia outside Israel, a claim unattributed at source

stops.name: Bombay, Albert takes the house
stops.date_confidence: the succession is attested to 1864; no month is given, and December is used to place it after the death
stops.campa: Albert Abdullah David Sassoon, the eldest, takes the firm. He is his father's opposite in every outward thing, English-speaking, English-dressed, easy in Government House, and he drives the business harder and further than his father did: mills, docks, a knighthood, a baronetcy, and in the end a move to England. Within three years his brother Elias will walk out and set up against him. The estate divides along the line the father held together by being alive.
suggested_refs: Sir Albert Abdullah David Sassoon, first baronet, and the Bombay mills

stops.name: Bombay, the marble statue on Rampart Row
stops.date_confidence: statue completed 1865; the library building around it was constructed 1867-1870
stops.campa: Sir Bartle Frere, Governor of Bombay, opens a subscription for a statue, and Thomas Woolner cuts it in marble within a year of the death: the old man standing, robed and turbaned, exactly as the English officials who subscribed had seen him. The money comes from the Jewish community, from traders, and from Englishmen together. The statue goes into a library and reading room on Rampart Row, built with sixty thousand rupees of his own money against a cost of a hundred and twenty-five thousand, the government finding the rest.
suggested_refs: Thomas Woolner's marble statue and bust at the David Sassoon Library, Fort, Mumbai

stops.name: Poona, the hospital opens on his bequest
stops.date_confidence: founding attested to 1867; the Gandhi appendectomy is attested to 12 January 1924
stops.campa: A hospital opens at Poona on his bequest, with room for a hundred and forty-four patients. It is open still, under his name in Marathi and in English, with close to thirteen hundred beds and a government medical college attached to it. Mohandas Gandhi will be cut for appendicitis on a table in this building in January 1924, a prisoner of the Bombay government at the time. His grandson Jacob will raise a second block beside it, tiled inside with nursery rhymes and fairy tales for the children.
suggested_refs: Jacob Sassoon Hospital, 1906-1909, with Royal Doulton tile panels by Margaret Thompson

stops.name: Bombay, the second house
stops.date_confidence: 1867 attested for the split; no month is given
stops.campa: Elias, who opened China and ran it for twenty years, quarrels with his brother over who commands what their father left, and goes out to found E.D. Sassoon and Company, offices in Bombay and Shanghai, in direct competition with the parent firm. The two houses will trade against each other for eighty years, and it is the breakaway one that ends up building the Bund. The family that came out of Baghdad as one household divides in three years over the succession.
suggested_refs: E.D. Sassoon & Co., founded 1867 in rivalry with David Sassoon & Co.

stops.name: Colaba, the wet dock and the fish market
stops.date_confidence: opened 1875, bought by the government for the Bombay Port Trust in 1879
stops.campa: Albert builds at Colaba the first wet dock on the western coast of India, so that ships can be worked at any state of the tide, and puts the family name on it. Four years later the government buys it for the Bombay Port Trust. It is called Sassoon Dock still, and it is working still: at four in the morning the Koli fishing fleet unloads there and half the city comes down to buy. Of everything the family built in Bombay, the thing that keeps the name in daily use is a fish market.
suggested_refs: Sassoon Dock, Colaba, and the St+art mural festival held there in 2017

stops.name: Galle, the death of the son who went east
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 March 1880; some accounts place the death at Colombo, which the source article contradicts
stops.campa: Elias David Sassoon dies at Galle in British Ceylon, on the harbor where the Indian Ocean routes bend for the Straits and China, sixty years old, the son who took the family east. His body goes back to Bombay for burial. Two years earlier he had opened a Jewish cemetery at Chinchpokli in memory of his own son Joseph, dead at Shanghai at the far end of the line his father had sent him down. The house he founded outlasts him, and in the end overshadows the one he was born into.
suggested_refs: The Chinchpokli Jewish Cemetery, Bombay, founded 1878; no coordinate was verifiable

stops.name: Fort, the grandson's synagogue
stops.date_confidence: 1884 attested; the builder is Jacob Elias Sassoon, grandson of David, and not the plural sons given in some summaries
stops.campa: Jacob Elias Sassoon builds a synagogue in the Fort, blue and white, in memory of his father Elias: Knesseth Eliyahoo, on the lane behind Kala Ghoda, by the architects Gostling and Morris. It is the second great Baghdadi synagogue of Bombay and the grandson's answer to the grandfather's at Byculla. Three generations out of Baghdad the family is still raising the same building, for a community that will begin leaving India within two generations more, mostly for London and for Israel.
suggested_refs: Knesseth Eliyahoo Synagogue, 55 Dr V.B. Gandhi Marg, Kala Ghoda, Fort

stops.name: Hove, the king comes to stay with the fifth son
stops.date_confidence: Arthur Sassoon lived at 8 King's Gardens from 1883 until his death in 1912; the royal visits are attested to 1898, 1907, 1908, and 1910
stops.campa: Arthur Sassoon, the fifth son, takes a house at 8 King's Gardens on the Hove seafront and lives in it for thirty years. Edward, Prince of Wales and afterwards King, stays there in 1898, in 1907, in 1908, and in 1910, partly for the sea air and largely because Alice Keppel is close by. Fifty years after a Baghdad refugee landed at Bombay with no English, the King of England takes his holidays in that man's son's house on the Sussex coast, and is glad of the invitation.
suggested_refs: 8 King's Gardens, Hove, Grade II listed; Albert's separate address at Eastern Terrace, Brighton

stops.name: Paris, the two banking houses joined
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the marriage is attested but the sources consulted give no date, and 1887, the year generally cited, is not independently verified here
stops.campa: Edward Albert Sassoon, grandson of the treasurer, marries Aline Caroline de Rothschild of the Paris house, daughter of Gustave. Two great Jewish financial families of the century are joined, one out of Frankfurt by way of London and Paris, one out of Baghdad by way of Bombay. Her kinswoman Bethsabee de Rothschild will be born into that same Paris line, and will leave the bank behind for modern dance in Israel. The Sassoon fortune is now inside the aristocracy of European money, three generations after it was carried out of a Mamluk city in the dark.
suggested_refs: The Sassoon-Rothschild marriage and the Paris branch of the Rothschild family

stops.name: City of London, the seat in the Commons
stops.date_confidence: Edward Albert Sassoon sat as a Conservative MP 1899-1912; Philip Sassoon held the seat 1912-1939
stops.campa: Edward Sassoon takes a seat in the House of Commons as a Conservative and holds it until he dies, and his son Philip takes the same seat after him and rises to Under-Secretary of State for Air. The family's business is done in the City now and its politics at Westminster, with the Bombay house a subsidiary of the London one in everything but law. Three generations after a wali of Baghdad ordered the family's head hanged, the family sits in the parliament that governs a quarter of the world.
suggested_refs: Sir Edward Albert Sassoon MP and Sir Philip Sassoon, Under-Secretary of State for Air

stops.name: Shanghai, Sassoon House on the Bund
stops.date_confidence: construction began 1926 and was completed 1929; renamed the Peace Hotel in 1956
stops.campa: Victor Sassoon, of the breakaway house, raises Sassoon House at the corner of the Bund and Nanjing Road, ten storeys of Art Deco under a green pyramid, with the Cathay Hotel inside it, begun in 1926 and finished in 1929 by the architects Palmer and Turner. It becomes the most famous building on the waterfront of the richest city in Asia. It is not the firm David Sassoon founded that builds it but the one his son Elias split away, so the grandest monument to the dynasty belongs to the quarrel.
suggested_refs: Sassoon House, later the Cathay Hotel, now the North Building of the Peace Hotel

stops.name: Alexandria, the branch put out of the country
stops.date_confidence: nationalizations from 1957, the expulsion of this branch attested to 1966; no month is given
stops.campa: The Egyptian branch, descended from David's brother Joseph, is stripped of citizenship and property after the nationalizations, and Elias Nissim Joseph Sassoon and his wife are taken down to the port of Alexandria and put out of the country. Across Asia the same thing happens in the same decades. Calcutta's Baghdadi community falls from about five hundred families to under a hundred, Rangoon loses its rabbi, and Baghdad itself empties of Jews entirely. The road he opened closes behind everyone who took it.
suggested_refs: Joseph Sassoon & Sons of Egypt, agents for Credit Foncier, and the 1966 expulsions

stops.name: Willemstad, the ledger comes to rest
stops.date_confidence: the Providence Group was formed in Switzerland in 1961 and moved to Curacao only in 1983; the common dating of the Curacao seat to 1961 collapses a 22-year gap
stops.campa: What is left of the Egyptian branch's capital, moved first into Switzerland in 1961, comes to rest at Curacao as an investment company. A hundred and fifty years after a fugitive treasurer stepped ashore at Bombay, the family money is a holding structure on a Dutch island in the Caribbean, and the ledger has traveled further than any of the men who kept it. The synagogues in Bombay and Poona are still standing, the dock still lands fish at dawn, and the hospital at Poona still takes patients under his name.
suggested_refs: The Providence Group, formed in Switzerland 1961, seated at Curacao from 1983
